What you will be able to do

  • Explain when separate triples form a connected RDF graph.
  • Distinguish the machine-readable graph from a node-link visualization.
  • Use shared governed identities to trace cross-system paths.
  • Test whether a competency question is answerable from the loaded statements.
  • Preserve source groups and unsupported boundaries in a Utility Mini-Graph.

Misconception we will change: A graph database or node-link picture is automatically a governed knowledge graph.

01
Relationship opening

The records exist. The answer path does not.

A Riverbend operations leader asks, "Which customer accounts are in the pressure zone served by Pump P-104, and which open work order could affect that service?" Geographic Information System records know the pump and zone. The customer system knows accounts and premises. Work management knows the repair. Each system can answer its own local question. None can yet show the complete route.

The missing thing is not another dashboard. It is a reviewed chain of statements that reuses the same governed identities across source boundaries. Until those statements meet, the utility has records but no defensible cross-domain path.

GIS knows Pump P-104 serves Zone 3, and the customer system knows Premise 882 has Account 882. What is still needed for the customer-exposure path?

Decision check

Choose the strongest answer, then check it. The feedback explains the boundary.

02
Representation distinction

The graph is the statements, not the drawing

In the Resource Description Framework, an RDF graph is a set of triples. A node-link diagram can help a person inspect those triples, but moving a circle on the screen does not change the graph. Adding, removing, or changing a statement does.

This distinction matters because a beautiful picture can hide weak identifiers, missing sources, vague predicates, or unsupported claims. Machine-readable statements need stable identifiers and explicit relationships. The display is only one projection of that underlying content.

Say each meaning aloud, then turn the card.

Flip-card retrieval

Say the answer before selecting each card. Select all four cards to complete this retrieval check.

03
Shared-node route

Reviewed identities let separate statements meet

Module 03 resolved which identifier denotes Pump P-104. That reviewed identity now becomes a meeting point. A geographic statement can say the pump serves Zone 3. A maintenance statement can say Work Order 4821 concerns the same pump. Neither source gives up its own record. The relationships join through the governed asset identity.

A shared label is not enough. The node must represent the same governed thing within the graph's scope. Once that condition is satisfied, every new statement can extend an existing path instead of creating another disconnected island.

Match each source statement to the relationship that lets the graph grow.

Relationship matching

Match each ordinary-language question to the job that answers it. Check all rows together, then revise any row that needs another look.

04
Graph Growth Laboratory

Grow the graph only until the questions become answerable

The laboratory begins with no statements loaded. Select each reviewed source packet and watch its triples enter the machine-readable ledger. The source label stays beside every statement, because connected does not mean source-free.

Test all three competency questions as you work. A failed test tells you which source packet is missing. It does not prove the real-world answer is false. It proves only that this bounded graph cannot yet support the answer.

05
Evidence path defense

Illuminate the exact route behind one answer

A graph answer is reviewable when you can name the path that supports it. For the customer exposure question, begin with Pump P-104, follow serves to Zone 3, contains to Premise 882, and hasAccount to Customer Account 882. Each edge answers one small part of the larger question.

Trace the path in order. Notice that no individual record contains the final answer. The answer emerges from several explicit statements that share governed nodes.

06
Practitioner view

Named source groups preserve where statements came from

An RDF dataset can organize graph content into a default graph and named graphs. In this lesson, the geographic, customer, maintenance, operational, and regulatory packets act as named source groups. That organization can help a query select, compare, or discuss particular graph content.

A named graph is not a truth stamp. The utility still needs provenance, effective time, authority, access control, review state, and correction procedures. Grouping statements makes source boundaries addressable. Governance determines how those groups may be trusted and used.

Which statements about named source groups are defensible?

Context boundary check

Select every item the bounded task needs. Leave irrelevant or unauthorized material outside the packet.

07
One Water transfer

Transfer the route to wastewater and stormwater

In wastewater, a response team may trace Lift Station 7 flowsTo Sewer Segment 44, Sewer Segment 44 upstreamOf Overflow Location 2, and Crew 6 assignedTo Incident 991. In stormwater, Inspection 55 occurredAt Catchment 5, Catchment 5 drainsTo Outfall 12, and Permit 8 appliesTo Outfall 12.

The graph is valuable when relationships are the question. If a single trusted table already answers the task, adding RDF may be unnecessary. Leaders should fund the graph where cross-system paths, shared meaning, provenance, reuse, or changing questions justify the added engineering and governance.

Which task most strongly justifies an RDF knowledge graph?

Decision check

Choose the strongest answer, then check it. The feedback explains the boundary.

Leader view

Ask which high-value questions repeatedly fail at system boundaries. Those questions define the first useful graph scope better than "build the enterprise graph."

08
Professional application

Build a mini-graph another team can challenge

Choose one bounded utility question. Record the source groups, governed nodes, explicit relationships, and the path that supports an answer. Then remove one edge mentally and state which answer becomes unsupported.

Name what your mini-graph cannot claim. This final boundary is part of the artifact, not a disclaimer added later. It keeps a useful answer from quietly becoming an unlimited assertion.

    Questions people actually ask

    Does every relationship belong in one graph?

    No. Include relationships that serve approved questions and uses. Separate domains or source groups may remain federated, restricted, or outside the graph.

    Is a graph database automatically a knowledge graph?

    No. A graph database stores graph-shaped data. A governed knowledge graph also needs shared meaning, identifiers, source controls, provenance, validation, ownership, and bounded uses.

    How large can a graph become?

    Technically, very large. The better design question is whether its partitions, mappings, queries, controls, and operating costs still serve the approved workload.

    Does a missing path mean the answer is false?

    Usually not. Under the open-world assumption, the graph may simply lack a required statement or source. Report unsupported or unknown unless a closed rule justifies false.

    Why keep source groups after connecting the graph?

    Source groups preserve attribution and let the utility apply different authority, freshness, access, and review policies to different statements.

    When is RDF unnecessary?

    If one governed source and a straightforward table query answer the stable task, RDF may add cost without enough value. Use it when explicit reusable relationships materially improve the work.

    Evidence boundary

    Riverbend Water, its records, and all answers are instructional. W3C RDF sources define RDF graphs, triples, datasets, and named graphs. They do not establish Riverbend's source authority, real asset state, customer exposure, or operational permission.

    Module Glossary

    RDF graph

    A set of Resource Description Framework triples.

    node

    A resource or value that participates in graph statements.

    edge

    A directed predicate relationship from a subject to an object.

    path

    A sequence of connected statements followed through a graph.

    shared node

    A governed resource identity reused by statements so separate paths can meet.

    graph visualization

    A human-readable display of graph content rather than the graph itself.

    RDF dataset

    A collection containing a default graph and zero or more named graphs.

    named graph

    An RDF graph associated with a graph name inside a dataset.

    competency question

    A specific question used to test whether a model or graph contains the required concepts and relationships.

    source group

    A bounded collection of statements kept attributable to a particular source or governance context.
